summaries.summary: Cyberbullying is defined by the National Crime Prevention Council, affects between to 10% to 40% of internet users, can cause effects from temporary anxiety to suicide, and includes Arvida Byström's October 2017 experience.

Cyberbullying detection is challenging due to subjective definitions, platform-specific semantics such as `fat' in the Twitter dataset, varying communication styles, evolving words and hashtags, and anonymity.

Past works have Bottleneck B1, Bottleneck B2, and Bottleneck B3, while this work targets Formspring, Twitter, and Wikipedia for personal attack, racism, and sexism using deep learning and transfer learning.

Experiments used logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, naive Bayes, CNN, LSTM, BLSTM, BLSTM with Attention, and bag of character n-gram, bag of word unigram, GloVe embeddings, SSWE embeddings.

Experiments used large, diverse, manually annotated, publicly available datasets from Formspring, Twitter, and Wikipedia talk pages, with class imbalance, vocabulary size variation, and truncation at the 95 percentile.

Formspring was a question and answer website whose dataset includes 12K annotated question and answer pairs, with 825 labeled as containing cyberbullying content by at least two Amazon Mechanical turk workers.
The Twitter dataset includes 16K annotated tweets, with 3117 labeled as sexist, 1937 as racist, and the remaining marked as neither sexist nor racist.
The Wikipedia dataset includes over 100k labeled discussion comments from English Wikipedia's talk pages, labeled by 10 annotators via Crowdflower, with 13590 comments labeled as personal attack.

Swear word usage and anonymity are inadequate cyberbullying clues, with 78% of Formspring swearing posts non-bullying, 82% of Twitter bullying posts lacking swear words, and Twitter disallowing anonymous postings.

Cyberbullying has been recognized since 2003, automatic detection since 2009, and existing text classification works rely on single SMP datasets, handcrafted features, F1 score, accuracy, and only recently deep learning.
Four DNN based models, CNN, LSTM, BLSTM, and BLSTM with attention, were tested with increasing neural architecture complexity and information use, differing only in the Neural Architecture layer.
The embedding layer used random, GloVe BIBREF12, and SSWE BIBREF13 initialization, learned task specific word embeddings, and reported results with dimension size 50 despite testing 30 to 200.

Models used dropout rates of 0.25 and 0.5, a fully connected layer, softmax, backpropagation, Adam, categorical cross-entropy, task-specific word embeddings, and code at https://github.com/sweta20/Detecting-Cyberbullying-Across-SMPs.
Traditional machine learning models LR, SVM, RF, and NB with character n-gram and word unigram representations performed significantly lower than DNN models across multiple SMPs.
All DNN models were implemented using Keras, with preprocessing removing stop words and punctuation marks and lowercasing, and performance reported after five-fold cross-validation.
Oversampling bullying posts thrice reduced class imbalance bias, improved all DNN models, especially Formspring with 825 bullying instances, and replication rate of three was good enough.
Initial word embeddings had no significant effect with oversampling, while without oversampling a performance gap between CNN and BLSTM with attention reduced as dataset size increased.
Table TABREF20 compares four DNN models using SSWE initial word embeddings, showing LSTM usually weaker and no significant performance gap among the other three models.
Learned embeddings from BLSTM with attention, visualized using t-SNE BIBREF16, show clusters of words relevant to particular cyberbullying topics in Table TABREF22.
Table TABREF23 shows word meanings change across cyberbullying topics, with Twitter treating slave as similar to racism and sexism targets, unlike Wikipedia.
Transfer learning was used with BLSTM with attention to test whether knowledge from one dataset improves cyberbullying detection on other datasets, with three flavors.

Complete Transfer Learning (TL1) gave significantly low recall, relatively higher precision, and showed Formspring and Wikipedia cyberbullying nature more similar than Twitter, with precision =0.51, recall=0.66, precision=0.38, and recall=0.04.
Feature Level Transfer Learning (TL2) transferred learned word embeddings to another dataset, dramatically improving recall and significantly improving precision over TL1.
Model Level Transfer Learning (TL3) transferred learned word embeddings and network weights but did not significantly improve over TL2, indicating learned word embeddings are key knowledge.
DNN based models with transfer learning beat best-known results, achieving F1 scores of 0.94 for Wikipedia and Twitter, and F1 score of 0.95 with accuracy score of 98% for Formspring.
DNN models with transfer learning beat state of the art results for all three datasets and may improve with profile, social graph, and severity information.
